[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"User-Defined Functions (UDFs) in SQL"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"User-Defined Functions (UDFs) are routines that you can define in SQL to perform specific tasks. They encapsulate complex logic and allow you to reuse that logic in multiple queries, making your SQL code more modular, readable, and maintainable. UDFs can accept input parameters and return a single value (scalar UDFs) or a table (table-valued UDFs)."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Types of User-Defined Functions"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"There are primarily two types of UDFs:"},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Scalar Functions: These functions return a single, scalar value (e.g., integer, string, date). They are suitable for performing calculations or transformations on input values."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Table-Valued Functions (TVFs): These functions return a table. They can be used to generate or filter data based on input parameters. There are two subtypes of TVFs: Inline TVFs and Multi-Statement TVFs."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Scalar User-Defined Functions"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"Scalar UDFs are the simplest type of UDF. They take zero or more input parameters and return a single value. The syntax for creating a scalar UDF is as follows:"},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"CREATE FUNCTION function_name (
    @parameter1 datatype1, 
    @parameter2 datatype2, 
    ...
)
RETURNS return_datatype
AS
BEGIN
    -- Function body (SQL statements)
    RETURN value
END;"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Let's create a scalar UDF that calculates the area of a circle given its radius:"},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"CREATE FUNCTION CalculateCircleArea (
    @radius DECIMAL(10, 2)
)
RETURNS DECIMAL(10, 2)
AS
BEGIN
    DECLARE @area DECIMAL(10, 2);
    SET @area = PI() * @radius * @radius;
    RETURN @area;
END;"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"To use the function, you can call it in a SELECT statement:"},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"SELECT dbo.CalculateCircleArea(5.0) AS CircleArea;"},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Table-Valued Functions (TVFs)"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Table-Valued Functions return a table as a result. They are useful for encapsulating complex queries that return multiple rows and columns."},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Inline Table-Valued Functions (ITVF)"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"Inline TVFs are defined with a single SELECT statement. They are similar to views but can accept parameters."},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"CREATE FUNCTION function_name (
    @parameter1 datatype1, 
    @parameter2 datatype2, 
    ...
)
RETURNS TABLE
AS
RETURN
(
    -- SELECT statement that defines the table
    SELECT column1, column2, ...
    FROM table_name
    WHERE condition
);"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"Here's an example of an ITVF that returns all customers from a specific city:"},{"order":20,"type":"code","text":"CREATE FUNCTION GetCustomersByCity (
    @city VARCHAR(50)
)
RETURNS TABLE
AS
RETURN
(
    SELECT CustomerID, CustomerName, City
    FROM Customers
    WHERE City = @city
);"},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"To use the function:"},{"order":22,"type":"code","text":"SELECT * FROM dbo.GetCustomersByCity('London');"},{"order":23,"type":"subheading","text":"Multi-Statement Table-Valued Functions (MSTVF)"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"Multi-Statement TVFs allow you to use multiple SQL statements to construct the table that is returned. They are more flexible than Inline TVFs but can be less performant."},{"order":25,"type":"code","text":"CREATE FUNCTION function_name (
    @parameter1 datatype1, 
    @parameter2 datatype2, 
    ...
)
RETURNS @table_variable TABLE
(
    column1 datatype1,
    column2 datatype2,
    ...
)
AS
BEGIN
    -- SQL statements to populate the table variable
    INSERT INTO @table_variable (column1, column2, ...)
    SELECT ...
    FROM ...
    WHERE ...

    RETURN;
END;"},{"order":26,"type":"paragraph","text":"Here's an example of an MSTVF that returns the order details for a specific customer:"},{"order":27,"type":"code","text":"CREATE FUNCTION GetOrderDetailsByCustomer (
    @customerID INT
)
RETURNS @OrderDetails TABLE
(
    OrderID INT,
    OrderDate DATETIME,
    ProductName VARCHAR(50),
    Quantity INT
)
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO @OrderDetails (OrderID, OrderDate, ProductName, Quantity)
    SELECT
        o.OrderID,
        o.OrderDate,
        p.ProductName,
        oi.Quantity
    FROM
        Orders o
    JOIN
        OrderItems oi ON o.OrderID = oi.OrderID
    JOIN
        Products p ON oi.ProductID = p.ProductID
    WHERE
        o.CustomerID = @customerID

    RETURN;
END;"},{"order":28,"type":"paragraph","text":"To use the function:"},{"order":29,"type":"code","text":"SELECT * FROM dbo.GetOrderDetailsByCustomer(123);"},{"order":30,"type":"subheading","text":"Benefits of Using UDFs"},{"order":31,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Modularity: UDFs break down complex logic into smaller, reusable units."},{"order":32,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Readability: UDFs make SQL code easier to understand and maintain."},{"order":33,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Reusability: UDFs can be called from multiple queries, reducing code duplication."},{"order":34,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Abstraction: UDFs hide the underlying implementation details, allowing you to focus on the higher-level logic."},{"order":35,"type":"subheading","text":"Considerations"},{"order":36,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Performance: MSTVFs can sometimes be less performant than Inline TVFs or regular SELECT statements. Consider performance implications when choosing between different types of UDFs."},{"order":37,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Deterministic vs. Non-Deterministic Functions: Deterministic functions always return the same result for the same input parameters. Non-deterministic functions may return different results even with the same inputs (e.g., functions that use `GETDATE()`). Use `SCHEMABINDING` option for deterministic functions to improve performance."},{"order":38,"type":"subheading","text":"Modifying and Deleting UDFs"},{"order":39,"type":"paragraph","text":"To modify a UDF, you can use the `ALTER FUNCTION` statement. The syntax is similar to `CREATE FUNCTION`."},{"order":40,"type":"code","text":"ALTER FUNCTION CalculateCircleArea (
    @radius DECIMAL(10, 2)
)
RETURNS DECIMAL(10, 2)
AS
BEGIN
    DECLARE @area DECIMAL(10, 2);
    SET @area = 3.14159 * @radius * @radius; -- More precise calculation
    RETURN @area;
END;"},{"order":41,"type":"paragraph","text":"To delete a UDF, use the `DROP FUNCTION` statement:"},{"order":42,"type":"code","text":"DROP FUNCTION dbo.CalculateCircleArea;"},{"order":43,"type":"paragraph","text":"By using UDFs effectively, you can write cleaner, more maintainable, and reusable SQL code."}]
